content: Asparagine, abbreviated as Asn or N, is one of the 20 most common naturally occurring amino acids on Earth. Its side chain contains a carboxamide functional group. It is classified as a non-essential amino acid, meaning the human body can synthesize it and it does not need to be obtained through the diet. Asparagine is encoded by the codons AAU and AAC. Asparagine was first isolated in 1806 from asparagus juice, where it is abundant, which is the origin of its name. It was the first amino acid to be isolated. The characteristic smell in urine after consuming asparagus is attributed to metabolic byproducts of asparagine. In 1891, Marceli Nencki suggested that methanethiol was responsible for this odor, while Robert White's 1975 research indicated that various thioesters were involved. Other potential contributors include asparagine aminosuccinic monoamide. Research by Allison and McWhirter in 1956 suggested that some individuals do not produce this odor after consuming asparagus, and this was thought to be autosomal. However, a re-examination in 1980 revealed that these individuals are instead unable to detect the odor. The side chain of asparagine can form efficient hydrogen bond interactions with the peptide backbone, making it frequently located near the beginning and end of alpha-helices and in turn motifs of beta-sheets in proteins. Its role is often described as capping hydrogen bond interactions that would otherwise need to be satisfied by the polypeptide backbone. Glutamine, which has an additional methylene group, is less effective in this role due to its greater conformational entropy. Asparagine also serves as a key site for N-linked glycosylation, a process where carbohydrate chains are added to the protein chain. Asparagine is not an essential amino acid, as it can be synthesized from intermediates in central metabolic pathways. Dietary sources of asparagine include animal products such as dairy, beef, poultry, eggs, fish, and seafood, as well as vegetarian sources like asparagus, potatoes, legumes, nuts, seeds, soy, whey, and whole grains. The biosynthesis of asparagine begins with oxaloacetate, which is converted to aspartate by a transaminase enzyme. This enzyme transfers an amino group from glutamate to oxaloacetate, producing α-ketoglutarate and aspartate. Asparagine synthetase then catalyzes the production of asparagine, AMP, glutamate, and pyrophosphate from aspartate, glutamine, and ATP. In this reaction, ATP activates aspartate to form β-aspartyl-AMP, and glutamine donates an ammonium group, which reacts with β-aspartyl-AMP to form asparagine and free AMP. Asparagine is degraded into aspartate and ammonium by the enzyme L-asparaginase, which hydrolyzes the amide group. Aspartate can then be converted back to oxaloacetate by a transaminase enzyme. Oxaloacetate can enter the citric acid cycle or be used in gluconeogenesis, as aspartate is a glucogenic amino acid. Asparagine plays a critical role in the nervous system, helping to maintain equilibrium and participating in amino acid transformation. It is also important in the synthesis of ammonia.
